assumptions.condition: \(X^{\mathrm{obs}}=X(0)\) almost surely on \(\{A=0\}\), and \(X^{\mathrm{obs}}=X(1)\) almost surely on \(\{A=1\}\).
\(\operatorname{TV}(k_{gx},k_x)\le d\) for every \(g\in\mathcal G\) and \(x\in\mathcal X\).

novel.justification: A deterministic total-variation radius measures the largest fraction of a four-state cross-world transition row that may be reassigned across trial populations. In commensurate trials using a common intervention, common endpoint definitions, and baseline-restricted populations, \(d\) is a prespecified sensitivity parameter whose full path can be reported. Randomized-arm marginals do not identify or bound this latent rowwise distance. Protocol or covariate similarity may motivate elicitation, but a proxy-to-TV bound is valid only under a separate explicit transport or validation assumption.

This observable open condition describes four trials with strictly positive but heterogeneous baseline prognosis-state mixtures. Such composition shifts arise when commensurate trials enroll different case mixes while no prognosis state is absent.

This observable restriction leaves a full neighborhood of positive stochastic matrices around a mechanism in which treatment commonly moves units into favorable surrogate states while endpoint responses remain mixed. It does not identify the latent positive TV radius.

assumptions.condition: Conditional on \(n_{ga}\), the \(2m\) vectors \(n_{ga}\widehat p_{ga}\) are mutually independent and each has the multinomial law \(\operatorname{Multinomial}(n_{ga},\pi_{ga}^{\mathrm{obs}})\).

standard.name: conditional independent multinomial sampling and \(L_1\) concentration

definitions.name: \mathfrak K_d(\mu^0,\nu)
definitions.construction: \(\mathfrak K_d(\mu^0,\nu)=\{\mathbf K: k_x\in\Delta_4\ \forall x\in\mathcal X,\ k_{gx}\in\Delta_4\ \forall g\in\mathcal G,x\in\mathcal X,\ \operatorname{TV}(k_{gx},k_x)\le d\ \forall g\in\mathcal G,x\in\mathcal X,\ \sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\mu_g^0(x)k_{gx}=\nu_g\ \forall g\in\mathcal G\}\).

definitions.name: (H_d^*,\mathcal R_{\mu,d}^*)
definitions.construction: \(H_d^*(h)=\max\{\sum_{g,x}\mu_g^0(x)\langle h_g,k_{gx}\rangle:k_x,k_{gx}\in\Delta_4,\ \operatorname{TV}(k_{gx},k_x)\le d\ \forall g,x\}\). Eliminate these row variables to obtain an irredundant half-space representation of the generated marginal polytope; after quotienting trialwise constant directions, \(\mathcal R_{\mu,d}^*\) is its finite set of nonzero facet-normal rays scaled to \(\ell_1\)-norm one.

definitions.name: (\Theta_g^{\mathrm{pr}}(d),L_g^{\mathrm{pr}}(d),U_g^{\mathrm{pr}}(d))
definitions.construction: \(\Theta_g^{\mathrm{pr}}(d)=\{N_g^{\mathrm{pr}}(\mathbf K)/D_g^{\mathrm{pr}}(\mathbf K):\mathbf K\in\mathfrak K_d(\mu^0,\nu)\}\), with \(L_g^{\mathrm{pr}}(d)=\min\Theta_g^{\mathrm{pr}}(d)\) and \(U_g^{\mathrm{pr}}(d)=\max\Theta_g^{\mathrm{pr}}(d)\) when this set is nonempty.

definitions.name: \Theta_g^{\mathrm{ST}}
definitions.construction: For \(\mathfrak J_g=\{J_g\in\mathbb R_+^{4\times4}:\sum_zJ_g(x,z)=\mu_g^0(x),\ \sum_xJ_g(x,z)=\nu_g(z)\}\), let \(\Theta_g^{\mathrm{ST}}\) be the range of \([\sum_{x:s_x=0,z:s_z=1}(y_z-y_x)J_g(x,z)]/[\sum_{x:s_x=0,z:s_z=1}J_g(x,z)]\) over \(J_g\in\mathfrak J_g\).

definitions.name: W^*
definitions.construction: Order states as \((0,0),(0,1),(1,0),(1,1)\). Set \(\mu^{\mathrm w}=10^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}7&1&1&1\\1&7&1&1\\1&1&7&1\\1&1&1&7\end{pmatrix}\), \(K^{\mathrm w}=40^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}2&2&18&18\\2&2&18&18\\1&1&19&19\\1&1&19&19\end{pmatrix}\), \(\nu^{\mathrm w}=\mu^{\mathrm w}K^{\mathrm w}\), and \(J^{\mathrm{alt}}=200^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}9&9&71&51\\0&0&20&0\\0&0&0&20\\0&0&0&20\end{pmatrix}\). The tuple of these four rational arrays is \(W^*\).

definitions.construction: \(\mathcal W_{\epsilon_{\mathrm w}}=\{(\mu^0,\nu):m=4,\ M\text{ is nonsingular},\ \max_{g,x}|M_{gx}-(3\mathbf 1\{g=\iota(x)\}/5+1/10)|<\epsilon_{\mathrm w},\ \max_{x,z}|[M^{-1}N]_{xz}-[40^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}2&2&18&18\\2&2&18&18\\1&1&19&19\\1&1&19&19\end{pmatrix}]_{xz}|<\epsilon_{\mathrm w}\}\).

definitions.name: (\mathcal C_{1-\alpha}^{\kappa},\widetilde\Theta_g,\mathcal I_{1-\alpha},\mathcal D_{1-\alpha}^{\mathrm{all}})
definitions.construction: Let \(\mathcal C_{1-\alpha}^{\kappa}\) contain every \(p\) with \(p_{ga}\in\Delta_4\), \(\|p_{ga}-\widehat p_{ga}\|_1\le\varepsilon_{ga}(\alpha)\), and \(\sum_{z:s_z=1}p_{g1}(z)-\sum_{x:s_x=1}p_{g0}(x)\ge\kappa\), for all \(g,a\). definitions.name: \mathsf{ProfileTV}
definitions.construction: Introduce variables for \(p_{g0}(x)k_{gx}(z)\), impose McCormick envelopes on recursively partitioned simplex boxes, retain direct simplex and rowwise total-variation constraints, solve nodewise Charnes--Cooper and sign-constrained relaxations, and branch on the product with the largest certified envelope gap.

statements.statement: Within every trial, randomization and consistency imply \(\pi_{g0}^{\mathrm{obs}}=\mu_g^0\) and \(\pi_{g1}^{\mathrm{obs}}=\nu_g\) for every \(g\in\mathcal G\).
statements.justification: This bridge identifies the potential-state marginals entering the kernel class from the observed randomized-arm laws.
statements.gap: The bridge is standard SUTVA identification, but stating it separately prevents a concentration inequality from carrying causal identification content.
statements.consumer: The endpoint and coverage theorems use the identified arm laws as the control and treatment marginals.

statements.statement: For every \(\mathbf K\in\mathfrak K_d(\mu^0,\nu)\), marginal reproduction gives \(D_g^{\mathrm{pr}}(\mathbf K)-R_g^{\mathrm{rev}}(\mathbf K)=\Delta_g^S\), so \(D_g^{\mathrm{pr}}(\mathbf K)\ge\Delta_g^S\ge\kappa\) for every \(g\).
statements.justification: The observable first stage, rather than latent entrywise positivity, totalizes every PSACE ratio.
statements.gap: JiangDingGeng2016 uses principal-stratum accounting, but the identity is required here uniformly over a shared-kernel sensitivity polytope.
statements.consumer: Every endpoint, sign-radius, and confidence-projection result uses this denominator bound.

For every \(d\in[0,1]\), \(\mathfrak K_d(\mu^0,
u)
eq\varnothing\) if and only if \[\sum_{g\in\mathcal G}\langle h_g,
u_gangle\le H_d^*(h)\quad	ext{for every }h\in(\mathbb R^4)^m.\] The right side is the direct rowwise polyhedral support in \(\mathrm{def:direct-support}\), and the finite normalized set \(\mathcal R_{\mu,d}^*\) suffices, including facets exposed at tied optima.
statements.justification: This gives exact compatibility directly from the unrestricted simplex-row TV polytope.
statements.gap: BeresteanuMolchanovMolinari2011 gives abstract support domination, while JiangDingGeng2016 imposes exact homogeneity; neither states this rowwise-TV shared-kernel marginal polytope.
statements.consumer: The cut test falsifies a radius and supplies the feasible set for the headline bounds.

statements.statement: After linearizing absolute values, fixed-radius compatibility is a linear program with \(O(mq^2)\) variables and constraints. Its dual returns either \(\mathbf K\) or a normalized violated cut. Rational inputs admit a rational feasible system or rational Farkas certificate of polynomial encoding length.
statements.justification: Finite exact certificates make the model auditable.
statements.gap: GalichonHenry2011 gives capacity checks for correspondences; this is the dual certificate for a distinct rowwise-TV kernel system.
statements.consumer: Meta-analysts can archive either latent rows or a reproducible failure certificate.

statements.statement: The minimum defining \(\rho^*\) is attained, \(\rho^*\in[0,1]\), and \(\mathfrak K_d(\mu^0,\nu)\neq\varnothing\) exactly when \(d\ge\rho^*\). At \(d=0\), every \(k_{gx}=k_x\), giving the ordinary linear image of the common row-stochastic kernel polytope without a rank or unique-facet condition.
statements.justification: This separates the observable-data compatibility threshold from the prespecified sensitivity radius and supplies the zero-drift sanity check.
statements.gap: WuMao2025 Corollary 2 identifies the exact common transition under full column rank but does not derive a minimum deterministic rowwise distance fitting potentially incompatible trials; randomized-arm marginals do not identify the latent cross-world drift.
statements.consumer: The ACCT analysis can report \(\rho^*\) as a fit diagnostic and lower bound while eliciting, rather than data-calibrating, the scientifically credible upper radius.

statements.statement: Whenever \(\mathfrak K_d(\mu^0,\nu)\neq\varnothing\), each coupled set is the attained interval \(\Theta_g^{\mathrm{pr}}(d)=[L_g^{\mathrm{pr}}(d),U_g^{\mathrm{pr}}(d)]\). Both endpoints are sharp over one common-center system fitting all \(m\) trials, and a Charnes--Cooper linear program returns each endpoint and an attaining \(\mathbf K\).
statements.justification: The headline delivers sharp attained PSACE endpoints while preserving cross-trial coupling.
statements.gap: WuMao2025 Corollary 2 is the primary zero-drift comparator: exact four-state transition transportability plus full column rank point-identifies the joint law and PSACEs, but it supplies no positive-TV identified set. JiangDingGeng2016 uses a different exact cross-trial homogeneity restriction or the without-monotonicity separate-trial bounds in arXiv Appendix A.1; YuanFellerMiratrix2018 instead uses zero site-level correlation, and WuAntonelli2024v1 instead uses continuous-intermediate outcome models with sign or dominant-observed-effect restrictions. The covariate-bound, proxy-identification, and historical-prediction comparators do not impose a shared cross-world rowwise-TV sensitivity class. CharnesCooper1962 supplies optimization machinery rather than this coupled latent class.
statements.consumer: An ACCT reanalysis can relax exact homogeneity and still report constructive sharp effects.

statements.statement: The observable marginals \((\mu^{\mathrm w},\nu^{\mathrm w})\) belong to \(\mathcal W_{\epsilon_{\mathrm w}}\). Every member of this class has strictly positive arm-state marginals, a strictly positive row-stochastic \(K^0=M^{-1}N\), and trial surrogate first stages exceeding \(13/100\); moreover the class contains a relative open neighborhood of \((\mu^{\mathrm w},\nu^{\mathrm w})\) in the product of the eight simplex interiors.
statements.justification: This verifies that the positive-radius comparison is a stable observable class result rather than a singleton witness calculation.
statements.gap: WuMao2025 proves point identification at exact transition transportability but does not give a nondegenerate observable neighborhood on which a positive TV relaxation remains informative.
statements.consumer: The strict-intermediate theorem uses this neighborhood to supply uniform positivity and slack.

statements.statement: For every \((\mu^0,\nu)\in\mathcal W_{\epsilon_{\mathrm w}}\), Wu--Mao's exact transportability model identifies \(K^0=M^{-1}N\) and \(\Theta_1^{\mathrm{pr}}(0)=\{\theta_1^{\mathrm{WM}}\}\). For every \(0<d\le\bar d=10^{-2}\), the rowwise-TV model obeys the two strict inclusions \[\{\theta_1^{\mathrm{WM}}\}=\Theta_1^{\mathrm{pr}}(0)\subsetneq\Theta_1^{\mathrm{pr}}(d)\subsetneq\Theta_1^{\mathrm{ST}}.\] Both strict gaps hold uniformly over this nondegenerate observable class.
statements.justification: This is the genuinely positive-radius headline: sensitivity relaxation adds ambiguity to the Wu--Mao point while cross-trial coupling still strictly sharpens a separate-trial analysis.
statements.gap: WuMao2025 Corollary 2 point-identifies the joint law and PSACEs under exact transportability and a full-column-rank condition, but gives no positive-radius partial-identification frontier. JiangDingGeng2016 arXiv Appendix A.1, Proposition A.4 gives without-monotonicity bounds trial by trial. LongHudgens2013 and MiratrixFureyFellerGrindalPage2017 sharpen principal-effect bounds with baseline covariates and principal-stratum restrictions, not cross-trial rows constrained around a shared kernel. The theorem supplies a strict two-sided comparison on an explicit observable neighborhood for every \(0<d\le10^{-2}\).
statements.consumer: An ACCT sensitivity analysis can distinguish small departures that invalidate point identification from larger departures that erase all pooling gains.

statements.statement:
For each \(g\), if \(\mathsf P_g(\mu^0,
u)\) is feasible, then \[\delta_{\mathrm{sign},g}=\min\mathsf P_g(\mu^0,
u)=\max_{(y,\lambda)\in\mathcal B_g(\mu^0)}\Phi_g(\mu^0,
u;y,\lambda)\in[0,1].\] The primal minimum and finite-cut maximum are attained; a primal optimizer contains an adversarial sign-reversing kernel, and a maximizing basic cut certifies that no smaller radius reverses the sign. If the primal is infeasible, then \(\delta_{\mathrm{sign},g}=+\infty\), and a Farkas ray certifies that no sign-reversing compatible kernel exists even at \(d=1\). For rational marginals, the optimizer, dual cut, or infeasibility ray can be chosen rational. Consequently \(\delta_{\mathrm{sign}}^{\mathrm{all}}=\min_g\delta_{\mathrm{sign},g}\), with the all-trial value equal to \(+\infty\) exactly when every trial has the infeasibility certificate.
statements.justification: The second headline turns robustness into an independently checkable primal--dual certificate rather than merely restating the radius definition.
statements.gap: HsiaoTianParast2025 studies resilience under single-study conditional-mean drift, and HsiaoParast2026 extends that object to a functional-class resilience probability learned from \(K\) completed studies for a new surrogate-only study. ElliottConlonLiKacirotiTaylor2015 uses trial-level causal-association random effects to estimate opposite-sign probabilities and a beneficial-surrogate threshold. ChenHarhayLi2026 uses principal-ignorability sensitivity bounds, while WuAntonelli2024v1 bounds continuous-intermediate model coefficients under same-sign or dominant-observed-effect restrictions. None targets a deterministic minimum latent rowwise shared-kernel TV distance to sign reversal across trial-specific PSACEs.
statements.consumer: The ACCT analysis can report how much heterogeneity is needed to overturn any trial.

statements.statement: If \(p^0\in\mathcal C_{1-\alpha}^{\kappa}\), then \(\widetilde\Theta_g(d;p^0)\subseteq\mathcal I_{1-\alpha,g}(d)\) for every \(g,d\), and \(\delta_{\mathrm{sign}}^{\mathrm{all}}(p^0)\in\mathcal D_{1-\alpha}^{\mathrm{all}}\). The inclusion also holds for \(\{\bot_{\mathrm{inc}}\}\) and \(+\infty\).
statements.justification: Coverage is reduced to deterministic inclusion without active-face regularity.
statements.gap: KaidoMolinariStoye2019 studies calibrated projection, not an augmented incompatibility fiber and extended-real radius.
statements.consumer: The sampling theorem applies this inclusion on the region-coverage event.

statements.statement: The observed-arm identification lemma and conditional multinomial concentration imply \(\Pr\{(\mu^0,\nu)\in\mathcal C_{1-\alpha}^{\kappa}\}\ge1-\alpha\). The set-inclusion lemma therefore gives simultaneous finite-sample coverage for all augmented PSACE fibers and \(\delta_{\mathrm{sign}}^{\mathrm{all}}\). The interval hull of each finite projected fiber covers both sharp endpoints whenever the true fixed-radius class is compatible. Coverage remains valid at tied cuts, at \(d\in\{0,1\}\), under incompatibility, and at \(+\infty\).
statements.justification: One maintained multinomial region yields tie-safe simultaneous inference.
statements.gap: ChoRussell2024 treats perturbed LP values, not projection over bilinear marginal--kernel products with incompatibility retained.
statements.consumer: The ACCT reanalysis can report simultaneous uncertainty for every endpoint and the all-trial radius.

statements.statement: Can \(\mathsf{ProfileTV}\) be completed into a face-complete algorithm computing exact finite endpoints of \(\mathcal I_{1-\alpha}(d)\) and the exact set \(\mathcal D_{1-\alpha}^{\mathrm{all}}\) for rational inputs while retaining \(\bot_{\mathrm{inc}}\) and \(+\infty\)? Characterize finite exact termination or give a certified \(\epsilon\)-termination bound uniform over active-cut ties.
statements.justification: Validity follows by inclusion, but varying control marginals with transition rows creates an unresolved bilinear computation.
statements.gap: McCormick1976 gives generic envelopes and ChoRussell2024 assumes linear moments; neither resolves this exact profile.
statements.consumer: A certificate would make the simultaneous analysis operational without discarding incompatible marginals or trusting local optima.

sampling_model.design: Independent randomized treatment assignment within each trial.
sampling_model.units: Conditional on arm sizes, observed states \(X^{\mathrm{obs}}\) are sampled independently within the \(2m\) trial--arm cells and yield multinomial empirical proportions.
sampling_model.treatment: Binary assignment \(A\), with both arms observed in every trial and SUTVA consistency linking the observed state to the assigned potential state.
sampling_model.overlap: Arm probabilities are positive and each observable surrogate first stage is at least \(\kappa\).
sampling_model.nuisance_estimation: The \(2m\) four-state marginals are empirical multinomial proportions profiled over \(\mathcal C_{1-\alpha}^{\kappa}\).

estimand_functional: \(\Theta_g^{\mathrm{pr}}(d)=[\min_{\mathbf K\in\mathfrak K_d}N_g^{\mathrm{pr}}(\mathbf K)/D_g^{\mathrm{pr}}(\mathbf K),\max_{\mathbf K\in\mathfrak K_d}N_g^{\mathrm{pr}}(\mathbf K)/D_g^{\mathrm{pr}}(\mathbf K)]\)

bibliography.citation: Imbens, G. W., and Rubin, D. B. (2015). \emph{Causal Inference for Statistics, Social, and Biomedical Sciences}. Cambridge University Press. Chapter 1 defines potential outcomes, assignment, and the stable-unit-treatment-value consistency relation.

Wu, P., and Mao, X. (2025). The promises of multiple experiments: identifying joint distribution of potential outcomes. arXiv:2504.20470v1, Section 6.2, Corollary 2. Under randomized assignment, transportability \(G\mathrel{\perp\!\!\!\perp}(S(1),Y(1))\mid(S(0),Y(0))\), and full column rank of the four-state control-marginal matrix, the four-state joint potential-outcome law and every PSACE are point identified. A revised article was published in \emph{Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B} (2026), DOI 10.1093/jrsssb/qkag118.

Jiang, Z., Ding, P., and Geng, Z. (2016). Principal causal effect identification and surrogate endpoint evaluation by multiple trials. \emph{Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B} 78(4), 829--848. The accessible journal record supports multi-trial identification under homogeneity and Bayesian sensitivity analysis in Section 7. The corroborating arXiv v1 has Proposition 2 on the necessary condition \(N_R\ge3\) for local identification without monotonicity and Appendix A.1, Proposition A.4 on separate-trial bounds without monotonicity; no unverified journal or online-supplement theorem numbering is asserted.
Yuan, L.-H., Feller, A., and Miratrix, L. W. (2018). Identifying and estimating principal causal effects in multi-site trials. arXiv:1803.06048v1. Section 4.1, Assumption 4.1, and Proposition 4.2.
Wu, M., and Antonelli, J. (2024). Partial identification of principal causal effects under violations of principal ignorability. arXiv:2412.06628v1. Sections 2.2.2, 4, and 5; Propositions 1--3.

Miratrix, L. W., Furey, J., Feller, A., Grindal, T., and Page, L. C. (2018). Bounding, an accessible method for estimating principal causal effects, examined and explained. \emph{Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness} 11(1), 133--162. DOI 10.1080/19345747.2017.1379576. The primary corroborating preprint is arXiv:1701.03139v2. Sections 3--4 construct principal-effect bounds under principal-stratum restrictions including monotonicity in the motivating setup; Sections 4--5 tighten bounds by stratifying and averaging over predictive baseline covariates; Section 7 applies the method across Early College High School sites.

Long, D. M., and Hudgens, M. G. (2013). Sharpening bounds on principal effects with covariates. \emph{Biometrics} 69(4), 812--819. DOI 10.1111/biom.12103. Sections 4--6 give single-trial monotonicity-based bounds, categorical-baseline-covariate tightening, and necessary and sufficient conditions for strict narrowing.

Trangucci, R., Chen, Y., and Zelner, J. (2024). Vaccine efficacy for binary post-infection outcomes under misclassification without monotonicity. arXiv:2211.16502, manuscript dated August 1, 2024. Assumptions 2.4--2.6 and Theorem 3.3 use site relevance, informative categorical baseline proxies, covariate and causal homogeneity, misclassification structure, and matrix or Kruskal-rank conditions for nonparametric point identification.
Beresteanu, A., Molchanov, I., and Molinari, F. (2011). Sharp identification regions in models with convex moment predictions. \emph{Econometrica} 79(6), 1785--1821. Theorem 2.1 and Section 5.
Galichon, A., and Henry, M. (2011). Set identification in models with multiple equilibria. \emph{Review of Economic Studies} 78(4), 1264--1298. Theorems 1--4.
Charnes, A., and Cooper, W. W. (1962). Programming with linear fractional functionals. \emph{Naval Research Logistics Quarterly} 9, 181--186. Theorems 1--3.
Hsiao, E., Tian, L., and Parast, L. (2025). Resilience measures for the surrogate paradox. arXiv:2506.12194. Sections 2--3.

Elliott, M. R., Conlon, A. S. C., Li, Y., Kaciroti, N., and Taylor, J. M. G. (2015). Surrogacy marker paradox measures in meta-analytic settings. \emph{Biostatistics} 16(2), 400--412. DOI 10.1093/biostatistics/kxu043. Sections 2--4 use a trial-level causal-association random-effects model to compute opposite-sign probabilities and a beneficial-surrogate-effect threshold.

Hsiao, E., and Parast, L. (2026). A functional-class meta-analytic framework for quantifying surrogate resilience. arXiv:2604.21020v1. Sections 2.1--2.2 and Theorem 1 use \(K\) completed surrogate-plus-outcome studies to infer a functional-class resilience probability in a new surrogate-only study under deviations from completed-study conditional-mean functions.

Baker, S. G., Sargent, D. J., Buyse, M., and Burzykowski, T. (2012). DOI 10.1111/j.1541-0420.2011.01646.x. Sections 2--4 fit historical-trial prediction models, including a principal-stratification option, and add leave-one-trial-out extrapolation error to predict the aggregate endpoint effect in a surrogate-only target trial.

Weissman, T., Ordentlich, E., Seroussi, G., Verd\'u, S., and Weinberger, M. J. (2003). Inequalities for the \(L_1\) deviation of the empirical distribution. Hewlett--Packard Laboratories Technical Report HPL-2003-97.
McCormick, G. P. (1976). Computability of global solutions to factorable nonconvex programs: Part I. \emph{Mathematical Programming} 10, 147--175.

comparator_promise_table.comparator_claim: ArXiv v1 Section 6.2, Corollary 2 point-identifies the four-state joint potential-outcome law and PSACEs under randomized assignment, exact transportability of the state transition from \((S(0),Y(0))\) to \((S(1),Y(1))\), and full column rank of the four-state control-marginal matrix.

ArXiv Appendix A.1, Proposition A.4 gives separate-trial PSACE bounds without monotonicity; arXiv Proposition 2 instead states that \(N_R\ge3\) is necessary for local identification without monotonicity.
Assumption 4.1 and Proposition 4.2 identify multi-site principal causal effects through zero site-level correlation between stratum prevalence and stratum-specific effects.
Propositions 1--3 partially identify continuous-intermediate model coefficients under parametric outcome models and same-sign or dominant-observed-effect restrictions.

The paper constructs principal-effect bounds under principal-stratum restrictions including monotonicity in its motivating setup and tightens them by stratifying and averaging over predictive baseline covariates in a multisite Early College High School application.
Sections 4--6 give single-trial monotonicity-based principal-effect bounds, categorical-baseline-covariate tightening, and necessary and sufficient conditions for strict narrowing.

Assumptions 2.4--2.6 and Theorem 3.3 use multicenter variation, informative categorical baseline proxies, homogeneity, misclassification, and rank conditions to point-identify post-infection principal effects.
Theorem 2.1 characterizes sharp convex prediction regions by support-function dominance.
Theorems 1--4 characterize finite-outcome compatibility through capacity inequalities.
Theorems 1--3 transform linear-fractional optimization into linear programming.

tldr: The model relaxes Wu and Mao's exactly transportable four-state transition kernel by coupling randomized ACCT trials through one shared stochastic center and primitive trial-specific stochastic rows within rowwise TV distance \(d\), with exact marginal reproduction. The radius \(d\) is a prespecified sensitivity parameter for latent cross-world rows, not a feature identified by randomized-arm marginals. The headline results give attained coupled PSACE intervals, an explicit nondegenerate observable class on which every \(0<d\le10^{-2}\) strictly enlarges the Wu--Mao point while remaining strictly sharper than separate-trial bounds, and a global sign radius characterized by an independent primal--dual cut system with rational certificates and a \(+\infty\) branch. Direct polyhedral support supplies compatibility, and an observable first stage bounds every denominator. Simultaneous multinomial coverage follows by set inclusion with incompatible candidate marginals retained, while exact bilinear profiling is open.

project_justification.gap: Wu and Mao point-identify four-state joint potential-outcome laws and PSACEs under exact transition transportability and full column rank, but do not characterize partial identification under a positive rowwise-TV relaxation. Jiang, Ding, and Geng identify PSACEs under a different exact cross-trial homogeneity restriction and give separate-trial bounds without monotonicity; Yuan, Feller, and Miratrix use a site-level zero-correlation restriction; Wu and Antonelli use continuous-intermediate outcome models with sign or dominant-observed-effect restrictions. Miratrix and coauthors and Long and Hudgens tighten principal-effect bounds using predictive baseline covariates under principal-stratum restrictions including monotonicity, while Trangucci, Chen, and Zelner obtain multicenter point identification from proxies, homogeneity, misclassification, and rank. The surrogate-resilience and historical-prediction comparators target different objects. None gives an attained positive-TV PSACE frontier together with a finite dual distance-to-sign-reversal certificate.
project_justification.niche: The missing object is a sensitivity path of coupled multi-trial PSACE intervals and distances to reversal, protected by an observable first stage and accompanied by compatibility certificates. The scientifically admissible upper range for \(d\) must be elicited rather than inferred from the trial marginals.
project_justification.fill: Randomization and consistency identify the kernel-class marginals from observed-arm laws, while conditional multinomial sampling supplies concentration. The direct rowwise support LP characterizes compatibility; linear-fractional programs attain endpoints over the full prespecified \(d\)-path; an explicit open observable neighborhood gives strict intermediate identification for every \(0<d\le10^{-2}\); and a canonical primal--dual sign program returns an adversarial kernel or a finite rational certificate. One maintained multinomial region gives simultaneous coverage by inclusion, and \(\rho^*\) remains only the smallest data-compatible radius.

related_work: Imbens and Rubin (2015, Chapter 1) supply the standard SUTVA consistency relation that, together with randomization, identifies potential-state marginals from observed arm laws; Weissman and coauthors (2003) are used only for multinomial \(L_1\) concentration. Wu and Mao (2025, arXiv v1, Section 6.2, Corollary 2) point-identify the four-state joint potential-outcome law and every PSACE under randomized assignment, exact transportability of the transition from \((S(0),Y(0))\) to \((S(1),Y(1))\), and full column rank of the control-marginal matrix. Their common-kernel result is the \(d=0\) boundary; the positive-radius neighborhood theorem strictly enlarges that point for every \(0<d\le10^{-2}\) while remaining strictly inside the separate-trial interval. Jiang, Ding, and Geng (2016) provide multi-trial identification under a different cross-trial homogeneity restriction and Bayesian sensitivity analysis for deviations from that homogeneity. In the corroborating arXiv v1, Proposition 2 is the necessary condition \(N_R\ge3\) for local identification without monotonicity; the separate-trial without-monotonicity PSACE bounds are instead in Appendix A.1, Proposition A.4. The positive-radius neighborhood theorem strictly tightens those separate-trial bounds without asserting an unverified journal or online-supplement theorem number. Yuan, Feller, and Miratrix (2018, Section 4.1, Assumption 4.1, and Proposition 4.2) identify multi-site principal causal effects under the strong condition that site-specific stratum prevalence is uncorrelated with site-specific stratum effects; they neither posit a shared cross-world transition kernel nor a TV sensitivity set. Wu and Antonelli (2024, arXiv v1, Sections 2.2.2, 4, and 5) partially identify principal effects using parametric continuous-intermediate and outcome models together with same-sign or dominant-observed-effect restrictions; their target and restrictions differ from the binary multi-trial shared-kernel model. Miratrix, Furey, Feller, Grindal, and Page (2018; arXiv:1701.03139v2) construct principal-effect bounds under their principal-stratum restrictions, including monotonicity in the motivating setup, and tighten them by stratifying and averaging over predictive baseline covariates in a multisite Early College High School application. They do not pool sites through one shared cross-world transition kernel, vary a rowwise-TV radius, characterize cross-site kernel compatibility, or produce a minimum sign-reversal radius. Long and Hudgens (2013, Sections 4--6) give single-trial monotonicity-based principal-effect bounds, categorical-baseline-covariate tightening, and necessary and sufficient conditions for strict narrowing. They neither leverage cross-trial or cross-site variation nor constrain trial-specific cross-world rows by distance to a shared kernel; their bounds therefore inform the separate-trial benchmark for the strict-improvement theorem rather than the generic LP machinery. Trangucci, Chen, and Zelner (2024, Assumptions 2.4--2.6 and Theorem 3.3) exploit multicenter variation, informative categorical baseline proxies, site relevance, covariate and causal homogeneity, misclassification structure, and matrix or Kruskal-rank conditions to nonparametrically point-identify post-infection principal effects. Their genuinely close proxy and tensor-decomposition model neither contains nor subsumes sharp binary PSACE intervals under prespecified shared-row TV drift, compatibility radii, or TV distances to sign reversal. Baker, Sargent, Buyse, and Burzykowski (2012, Sections 2--4) fit historical-trial prediction models, including a principal-stratification option, and add leave-one-trial-out extrapolation error to predict the aggregate endpoint effect in a target trial observing only the surrogate. Their adjacent multi-trial prediction target does not identify or sharply bound within-principal-stratum effects through a common kernel and does not deliver a deterministic TV sensitivity or sign-radius path. Beresteanu, Molchanov, and Molinari (2011, Theorem 2.1) inform the support formulation, but the support here remains the direct rowwise-TV LP. Galichon and Henry (2011, Theorems 1--4) inform finite certificates without representing this kernel. Charnes and Cooper (1962) inform endpoint computation after the observable first-stage identity establishes positivity. Elliott, Conlon, Li, Kaciroti, and Taylor (2015, Sections 2--4) use a trial-level causal-association random-effects meta-analytic model to compute probabilities of opposite-sign surrogate and endpoint effects and a beneficial-surrogate-effect threshold. They do not target individual principal-stratum effects, a latent cross-world kernel identified set, or a deterministic minimum rowwise-TV perturbation. Hsiao, Tian, and Parast (2025) study resilience under controlled conditional-mean drift in a single prior-study setting. Hsiao and Parast (2026, Sections 2.1--2.2 and Theorem 1) directly extend that object to \(K\) completed surrogate-plus-outcome studies and infer a functional-class resilience probability for a new surrogate-only study under deviations from completed-study conditional-mean functions; this object is not a trial-specific PSACE bound or a shared latent transition-kernel TV radius. Chen, Harhay, and Li (2026) inform sensitivity motivation through principal-ignorability deviation bounds, a different deviation class and estimand. Kaido, Molinari, and Stoye (2019), Cho and Russell (2024), and McCormick (1976) inform projection and the open profiling route.
technical_internal_limitation: Varying \(p_{g0}(x)\) jointly with \(k_{gx}(z)\) creates bilinear products. Finite-sample validity does not require solving this problem, but exact global profiling and useful complexity guarantees remain open. The randomized-arm marginals identify the compatibility threshold \(\rho^*\), not the latent rowwise distance or a scientifically credible upper sensitivity radius.
honest_scope: Centers and trial rows are primitive unrestricted simplex points for every control state; a trial row is interpreted as a conditional law only on control states with positive mass. No latent entry floor is imposed. Randomization and SUTVA consistency identify the potential-state marginals with the observed arm laws, and denominator positivity comes only from the maintained observable first stage. Compatibility uses the direct support LP. The radius \(d\) bounds latent cross-world rows, is not identified from randomized-arm marginals, and is prespecified for sensitivity analysis. The practical regime is a collection of commensurate trials with a common intervention, common endpoint definitions, and baseline-restricted populations; protocol or covariate similarity may motivate elicitation but does not identify or bound rowwise TV. The full endpoint and sign-robustness path is reported over \(d\in[0,1]\), with incompatible radii retained and \(\rho^*\) interpreted only as an observable-data compatibility diagnostic. Wu and Mao's point-identifying model is the \(d=0\) full-rank boundary; the strict positive-radius result is limited to the explicitly defined observable neighborhood and \(0<d\le10^{-2}\). Fixed-margin endpoints, primal--dual sign certificates, and conservative coverage are theorem targets; exact bilinear confidence-region profiling and the numerical ACCT reanalysis remain open.
